Senses.Explanation: Green mountains fill the eyes means that green mountains occupy the whole field of sight. Tiantai Deshao's verse joins the line to ‘outside mind there is no thing.’ Guizong Zhichang turns the view toward Nanquan; Baiyu Jingsi answers a question about leakage with green mountains free of dust; and Zhuanyu Guanheng places them in a verse on what remains when nothing further is known within mind. An unnamed monk asks Yi'an Shanzan whether birds, flowers, and mountains filling the eyes are the dwelling of the immeasurable person. Juean Mengzhen raises Deshao's verse and objects that it has been broken into two pieces; Huangbo Xiyun uses the same line while refusing added interpretations of sights and sounds.

“Filling the eyes and ears” coordinates sight and hearing as an already pervasive presentation. Hongzhi Zhengjue says it is so throughout the twelve periods, then asks whether the assembly recognizes it. Buhui Fatong uses the pair in a verse that denies separation or combination. Baichi Xingyuan joins it to what is present everywhere, while Chushi Fanqi uses it as a substitute answer and immediately warns against mistaking servant for master.
Senses.Note: Keep eye and ear together. Ordinary claims that sights or sounds are plentiful do not by themselves carry this coordinated Chan use.

Senses.Explanation: Moonlight fills an otherwise empty boat while a fisherman sleeps by the reeds. Furong's original answer meets the question of what is visible at midnight but hidden at dawn; Eryin explains its two movements. Liangting, Chulin, and Danxia give distinct verses that revisit the boat, moon, and changing light.

Senses.Explanation: To be shamefaced and alarmed is to be visibly exposed and abashed; Chan speakers and verse authors repeatedly predict or portray that reaction when a position cannot be sustained. A transmitted Shakyamuni verse portrays him shamefaced after losing his former eyes. Tian'an Sheng says Huangbo would have been left shamefaced without Linji's ability to receive the blows. Chulin Shangrui says an immediate laugh would leave Linji shamefaced despite his strengths. Baiyu predicts that a short reply to Mazu's illness saying would leave the target shamefaced with nowhere to put himself. These occurrences support the exposed reaction while preserving the distinct case circumstances.

Senses.Note: The pole belongs to a traveling performance image: one carries what is needed, then performs where an occasion appears. Deng Yinfeng answers Mazu with the full pair before visiting Shitou. Baichi uses that image when his sermon becomes another performance; Baiyu, Feiyin, Faxi, Chaozong, and Xixin apply it to their own responses. Senses.Explanation: The pole-top move is the move asked for after someone has already reached the top of a hundred-foot pole. The records do not fix it as literal forward motion: they answer it through turning, release, and even retreat. Changsha Jingcen's verse says that the person unmoving atop the hundred-foot pole has gained entry but is not yet real, then calls for a further move and says that the worlds in the ten directions are the whole body (百尺竿頭不動人雖然得入未為真百尺竿頭須進步十方世界是全身). In The Gateless Barrier, 竿頭進步 is the editorial title above Shishuang Qingzhu's question, not words attributed to Shishuang himself. The phrase then circulates in questions and comments: Yexian Guixing answers with the southern and northern continents; Linye Qi answers “retreat and then it is attained” (退後即得); and Shanduo Zhenzai answers with a beheaded boatman going down to Yangzhou. Wansong Xingxiu pairs the pole-top move with release at the point of holding fast, while Langye Huijue sets it beside turning and breathing out. These uses preserve the pole-top image but refuse to reduce 進步 to ordinary forward travel.
